newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU dumping committee to meet on Norwegian salmon.
newsitem.headline: EU dumping committee to meet on Norwegian salmon.

text.p: The European Union's anti-dumping committee will meet on Monday to discuss a European Commission proposal to impose a duty on imports of farmed Atlantic salmon from Norway, an EU source said on Thursday.
The EU executive is proposing a duty of, on average, 13.7 percent on imports of Norwegian salmon, accusing Norwegian producers of dumping and of receiving state subsidies, the source said.
"I'm very surprised and disappointed," Norwegian Fisheries Minister Karl Eirik Schuett-Pedersen was quoted as saying in Swedish daily Dagens Nyheter earlier this week.
Norway is a member of the 18-nation European Economic Area but its voters rejected EU membership in a 1994 referendum.
The anti-dumping committee, which consists of officials from EU member states, can only give advice on this issue.
It is the Commission which has the power to impose provisional duties for six months, but it may take into account the opinions of member states before taking a final decision.
In September, the Commission said it was looking into Scottish complaints that imports of salmon from Norway were being subsidised and dumped, hurting the EU industry.
The EU executive decided to open separate anti-dumping and anti-subsidy investigations concerning imports of farmed Atlantic salmon from Norway.
The Scottish Salmon Growers' Association Ltd and the Shetland Salmon Farmers' Association lodged the complaints.
Norwegian sources have rejected the dumping allegations, saying that Norwegian producers were just more efficient than those elsewhere.
If the Commission decided to slap an import duty on Norwegian salmon, this would amount to a protectionist measure, one Norwegian source told Reuters last month.
The Financial Times newspaper reported in March that a confidential report by Commission experts said that Norwegian producers have been selling salmon in the EU at less than the cost of production.
The report also said that Norwegian producers had been paid unfair state subsidies, causing prices to fall and Scottish salmon growers to lose profits, the paper said.
